clue.text: Deceased I examine wither and dissolve (in bardic parlance)

parts.note: d. is the abbreviation for died or deceased
taken as written
to scan is to examine closely
plants die or wither away

explanation.surface: A grim line about a dead speaker who studies something as it withers and melts away.
explanation.walkthrough: The bard is Shakespeare, who used discandy in Antony and Cleopatra; Chambers gives this spelling as a variant.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's verb means to melt away or dissolve, as candy does; the bracket marks it as his own usage.

clue.text: Fine work from Brussels about the French Roquefort mould of top quality? (12, two words)

parts.note: du is French for of the, as in talking about the thing
a chessel is a cheese mould, and Roquefort is a cheese
ace means first-rate

explanation.surface: A query whether the prized blue mould in French Roquefort counts as fine Belgian craftsmanship.
explanation.walkthrough: Roquefort and mould pull towards the blue veins in the cheese; mould here is the vessel cheese is pressed in.
explanation.definitionFit: Duchesse lace is a fine Flemish bobbin lace made in Brussels and Bruges, so it is delicate needlework from Brussels.

clue.text: People shortly taking possession of Hungary

indicators.note: to take possession of something is to hold it, so one piece is held inside another

parts.note: in a bit means soon, shortly
H is the international vehicle code for Hungary

explanation.surface: Settlers will soon be taking over Hungary.
explanation.walkthrough: People looks like a plural noun, but it is the verb meaning to populate a place.
explanation.definitionFit: To people a land is to fill it with inhabitants, which is to inhabit it.

clue.text: Walk unsteadily, as qualified doctor in graduation?

indicators.note: in places the doctor inside the word that follows

parts.note: a graduation is a mark on a measuring scale
MB, Bachelor of Medicine, is a doctor's qualifying degree

explanation.surface: A newly qualified doctor staggers about at the graduation ceremony.
explanation.walkthrough: Graduation suggests a degree ceremony, which fits the doctor; it is a mark on a scale. Shamble is the tempting wrong guess.
explanation.definitionFit: Scamble is a dialect word meaning to stumble or shamble along, so it is to move unsteadily.

clue.text: X, algebraic variable giving schoolboy nuisance

parts.note: chi is the Greek letter written X
x, y and z are the standard unknowns in algebra

explanation.surface: An algebra lesson's unknown x is just an irritation to a schoolboy.
explanation.walkthrough: Chiz is schoolboy slang from the Molesworth books by Geoffrey Willans, meaning a swindle or annoyance.
explanation.definitionFit: In Molesworth's schoolboy slang a chiz is a swizz or cheat, the kind of nuisance a pupil grumbles about.

clue.text: Considerable wind after consuming starter of haricots in eatery

definitions.text: Considerable wind after consuming starter of haricots in eatery

indicators.note: something consumed goes inside, so one letter is swallowed by the other word

parts.note: a noser is a strong headwind

indicators.note: a starter comes first, so only the opening letter is taken

parts.note: the first letter of the bean

explanation.surface: A diner suffers flatulence after tucking into a plate of beans at a restaurant.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue describes the answer: an eater in a restaurant who has had beans and now has wind.
explanation.definitionFit: A nosher is slang for an eater, someone who noshes, and the clue pictures one in a restaurant.

clue.text: Measure maybe suggested by party (green)

parts.note: a do is a party
sage green is a greyish green

explanation.surface: A political party with green leanings proposes a new measure.
explanation.walkthrough: Measure and party suggest politics; the measure is a quantity of medicine.
explanation.definitionFit: A dosage is a measured amount of medicine, so it is one kind of measure.

clue.text: Submerge limb attached to training rope

parts.note: a limb, as in a limb of Satan, is a mischievous child or imp
a lunge is a long rope used in training horses

explanation.surface: An instruction to dunk an arm tied to a training rope underwater.
explanation.walkthrough: Limb looks like an arm or leg; it is the old sense of a naughty child.
explanation.definitionFit: Implunge is an old word meaning to plunge in or immerse, which is to submerge.

clue.text: Large hairy dog, tail disappearing in pipe

indicators.note: the tail of a word is its final letter, which vanishes here

parts.note: the briard is a large, long-haired French sheepdog

explanation.surface: A shaggy dog's tail vanishes down a drainpipe.
explanation.walkthrough: Tail looks like the dog's real tail, but it means the last letter of the breed.
explanation.definitionFit: A briar is a tobacco pipe carved from the root of the tree heath.

clue.text: Sentimentality about place one associates with Wellington? That's absurd

indicators.note: about means around, so one word wraps round the other

parts.note: goo is sickly sentimentality
Wellington is the capital of New Zealand

explanation.surface: Getting gushy about the Duke of Wellington is ridiculous.
explanation.walkthrough: Wellington suggests the duke or the boot; here it is the capital city.
explanation.definitionFit: Gonzo means bizarre or crazy, so something gonzo is absurd.

clue.text: Stint with harpoon at sea? It's aimed to get back at adversary

definitions.text: It's aimed to get back at adversary

indicators.note: at sea means confused and all over the place, so the letters are muddled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A whaler's spell with a harpoon, aimed back at the creature attacking him.
explanation.definitionFit: An antistrophon is an argument turned back against the opponent who made it, a rhetorical retort.

clue.text: Ring for sailing boat's timber, blessing when securing painter

indicators.note: to secure something is to hold it fast, here by enclosing one word inside another

parts.note: a boon is a blessing or benefit
Joan Miró, the Spanish painter

explanation.surface: A sailor asks for a ring on a boat's spar, hoping for good fortune while the mooring rope is made fast.
explanation.walkthrough: On a boat a painter is a mooring rope, which suits the surface; here it is the artist Miró, slotted into BOO-N to give BOOMIRON.
explanation.definitionFit: A boom-iron is the metal hoop on a yard through which a studding-sail boom slides, so it is a ring fitted to a ship's spar.

clue.text: Spinach, not pressure cooked, connected courses

indicators.note: cooked food is mixed and altered, so the remaining letters are jumbled
not tells us one letter of the vegetable is to be left out

parts.note: taken as written
P is the symbol for pressure

explanation.surface: Spinach served raw rather than steamed under pressure, as part of a linked series of dishes.
explanation.walkthrough: Courses looks like the courses of a meal, which suits the spinach; here it means a run of linked things.
explanation.definitionFit: A chain is a series of linked units, so chains are courses or sequences joined end to end.

clue.text: Run second edition

parts.note: s is the abbreviation for second
a print or printing is an edition of a book

explanation.surface: An instruction to put a second printing of a book through the presses.
explanation.definitionFit: To sprint is to run at full speed over a short distance.

clue.text: Stop sign? Hospital nurse skirts zone

parts.note: H is the map abbreviation for a hospital

indicators.note: to skirt something is to go round its edge, so one word wraps around another

parts.note: an amah is a nurse or maid in the Far East
Z is an abbreviation for zone

explanation.surface: A traffic sign outside a hospital where a nurse steers round a restricted zone.
explanation.walkthrough: The stop is a glottal stop, not a road sign; the question mark warns of the twist.
explanation.definitionFit: Hamzah is the Arabic letter-mark for a glottal stop, so it is a written sign for a stop.

clue.text: It's essential to check a zip … after visit here?

definitions.text: It's essential to check a zip … after visit here?

indicators.note: essential means at the core, so the letters sit inside the following words

parts.note: the middle letters of these three words

explanation.surface: Sound advice to do up your flies after a trip to the loo.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the hiding place and the definition: a kazi is British slang for a lavatory, where you check your zip afterwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Kazi is slang for a lavatory, the place after visiting which one checks one's flies.

clue.text: Vintners were awaiting vintage variety of rouges

parts.note: bode is an old past tense of bide, to wait for

indicators.note: a variety is a different version, so the letters of the wine word are made into another form

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Wine merchants are waiting for a new vintage of red wines to arrive.
explanation.walkthrough: Were awaiting looks like plain surface tense; it is BODE, the archaic past of bide.
explanation.definitionFit: A bodeguero is a Spanish wine merchant or cellar owner, so the plural means vintners.

clue.text: Bishop separates man and lady falling out in hateful fashion

indicators.note: something that separates comes between parts, so it sits inside the other letters
a couple falling out are thrown into disorder, so their letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
B is the chess abbreviation for bishop

explanation.surface: A bishop comes between a quarrelling couple who are being horrible to each other.
explanation.definitionFit: Damnably is an adverb meaning detestably or abominably, which is in a hateful way.

clue.text: Residue left in position?

indicators.note: in places one letter inside the word that follows

parts.note: the sit of a garment is the way it is positioned or hangs
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A question about whatever residue has been left where it was.
explanation.definitionFit: Silt is the fine sediment left behind by water, so it is a deposited residue.

clue.text: Excited parent, in ecstasy

indicators.note: excited things are stirred up and agitated, so the letters move about

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A thrilled mother or father, carried away with joy.
explanation.definitionFit: Enrapt means rapt or enraptured, that is, carried away in ecstasy.

clue.text: Distant point in a space orbit, or one in an opposite extreme

definitions.text: Distant point in a space orbit

parts.note: an is the indefinite article

indicators.note: in places the number word inside the extreme

parts.note: the poles are opposite extremes
un is French for one, also dialect for one

explanation.surface: An astronomy note: the far point of an orbit, or a point at the opposite end of something.
explanation.definitionFit: Apolune is the point in a lunar orbit farthest from the moon, a distant point of a spacecraft's path.

clue.text: Coarse sugar transformed capon — what a surprise!

indicators.note: transformed means changed into a different form, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
ha is an exclamation of surprise

explanation.surface: A cook is amazed to find a chicken turned into a lump of sugar.
explanation.definitionFit: Panocha is a coarse brown Mexican sugar, also a fudge made from it.

clue.text: Poet's circle, checked, finally died away

indicators.note: the closing letters fade out, so the ending of the word is dropped

parts.note: to stem a flow is to check it

explanation.surface: A poet's circle of friends was held back and in the end faded out.
explanation.walkthrough: The poet is Spenser, whose stemme meant to encircle; the past-tense ending of checked dies away. The blog's grid shows STEMME, losing only the D.
explanation.definitionFit: Spenser used this verb for encircling or surrounding, so it is a poet's word for to circle.

clue.text: Jenny's cake? That won't last long!

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the cream cake that shares its name with the comedian Jenny ...
second meaning: French for a lightning flash, gone in an instant

explanation.walkthrough: Jenny Eclair is a British stand-up comedian and Radio 4 regular, so her name is a pastry. The second half also jokes that such a cake is soon eaten.
explanation.definitionFit: The cake is a finger of choux pastry with cream; the French word means a flash of lightning, which is brief.

clue.text: A gas created by transposing two single elements of a salt

indicators.note: transposing two letters swaps their places, a minimal rearrangement

parts.note: a saline is a salt, especially a medicinal one

explanation.surface: A chemistry note: a gas formed when two atoms in a salt change places.
explanation.walkthrough: Elements suggests chemical elements, which fits the gas; they are single letters, the A and the I.
explanation.definitionFit: Silane is silicon hydride, a colourless gas, the silicon counterpart of methane.

clue.text: Shut crystal ornament box

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an old verb for to bolt or fasten shut
second meaning: a crystalline mineral, polished for ornaments
third meaning: to box, as in practice bouts

explanation.surface: An instruction to close a box holding a crystal trinket.
explanation.walkthrough: Three separate meanings of one short word, strung together to read as a single sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is an obsolete verb for fastening, a lustrous mineral used decoratively, and the verb for light boxing.

clue.text: Cattle farmer, English, cooked nice roast

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for English

indicators.note: cooked food is mixed and changed, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An English rancher served up a pleasant joint of beef.
explanation.definitionFit: An estanciero owns or runs an estancia, a large South American cattle ranch.

clue.text: A cluster of spore cases in Eumycetes or Ustilago

indicators.note: in says the letters lie inside the words that follow

parts.note: the end of the first word, the second word and the start of the third

explanation.surface: A botanical note on spore clusters found in fungi and smut fungi.
explanation.definitionFit: A sorus is a clump of sporangia, as on a fern frond or a fungus.

clue.text: Swell: see me yielding to king suggesting royal sport?

indicators.note: yielding to means giving way, so one part gives up its place to another

parts.note: to tumefy is to swell
taken as written
R is short for rex, king

explanation.surface: A posh toff invites you to watch him lose to the king at some regal pastime.
explanation.walkthrough: Swell looks like a noun for a dandy; it is the verb. Horse racing is the sport of kings, run on the turf.
explanation.definitionFit: Turfy means of or like the turf, the world of horse racing, which is called the sport of kings.

clue.text: French town becomes foul with this hooligan?

parts.words: French town becomes foul with this hooligan?
parts.note: surface reading: a thug spoils a town in France
setter's reading: the French word for town, ville, becomes vile once one of its letters is taken away

explanation.surface: A yob's antics leave a pleasant French town looking a mess.
explanation.walkthrough: Ville is French for town; with an L removed it reads vile, meaning foul. So the answer, read as two parts, is the instruction L OUT.
explanation.definitionFit: A lout is a rough, uncouth young man, a synonym for a hooligan.

clue.text: Lines penned by Hank, idle

indicators.note: something penned is shut in an enclosure, so these letters go inside another word

parts.note: a hank of yarn is a coil or loop
L is the abbreviation for line, doubled for the plural

explanation.surface: A lazy writer named Hank produced a few lines.
explanation.walkthrough: Hank looks like a man's name; it is a coil of thread.
explanation.definitionFit: To lollop is to lounge about lazily, so it means to idle.

clue.text: Hill, flat on top, a creature responsible for one almost climbs

indicators.note: in a down answer climbing means reading from bottom to top
almost means not quite all, so the last letter is cut off

parts.note: taken as written
a mole makes a molehill, one being a hill

explanation.surface: A burrowing animal that made a flat-topped hill almost manages to clamber up it.
explanation.walkthrough: One refers back to Hill: a mole is the creature that makes a molehill.
explanation.definitionFit: A loma, in the American South-West, is a hill with a broad flat top.

clue.text: Roughly 20 pounds porter finally loaded into carriage

indicators.note: goods loaded into a vehicle end up inside it

indicators.note: finally points to the closing letter of the word it qualifies

parts.note: the last letter of the word

clue.text: Guarantee expired? Our vac (not right) needs replacing, getting hot

indicators.note: replacing the parts means putting them back in a new order
not right says the letter standing for right is left out

parts.note: taken as written
R is the abbreviation for right
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on taps

explanation.surface: The vacuum cleaner's warranty has run out, and it is overheating, so it must be replaced.
explanation.walkthrough: Expired with its question mark flags that the defining sense is archaic: avouch for guarantee is now obsolete.

clue.text: 'Ector in chokey requiring wrist fastener (one of a pair) (8, two words)

indicators.note: in places the bully inside the jail word

parts.note: chokey and clink are both British slang for prison
to hector is to huff or bully; the dropped H of 'Ector says drop it from huff too

explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe shows a dropped aitch, so hector becomes 'uff, a cockney huff.
explanation.definitionFit: A cufflink fastens a shirt cuff at the wrist, and they are worn in pairs.

clue.text: Yearn to wander wrapped in fur of mountain region

parts.note: taken as written
